title: The Council of Trent (1545–63)
hook: Catholics reform seminaries, clarify teaching, and renew the Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, Latimer and Ridley burned together, and a line the story leaves for us: never again. Who across a divide did you wish well, or say one human thing about? Day eight hundred seventy-two.

What, exactly, does the Catholic Church teach, and what in its own life needs fixing? That question has been tearing the Western church apart. To answer it, bishops arrive in a city in the mountains of northern Italy, where the road climbs toward the Alps, along with theologians and representatives of kings, their servants, their books and their arguments. The council opens. Then it breaks off. Then it meets again, and breaks off again, and meets again, over long years and more than one pope. The city's name is Trent. Today's word is the name later given to the whole movement around it: Counter-Reformation.

Start with the name. Counter-Reformation sounds like a punch thrown back, and part of Trent was exactly that: an answer to Luther, Zwingli and Calvin. Some historians prefer another name, the Catholic Reformation, because some Catholics had been calling for reform of their own church before anyone left it, and because much of what Trent did was cleaning house. So it did two things at once. First, it said clearly what Catholics hold. Scripture and tradition, received together. The sacraments, defined one by one. How a person is made right with God: by grace, received in faith, and lived out in works. Protestant churches answered much of this differently; Catholics receive these decrees as the teaching of a general council of the church. Second, it turned inward. Bishops were told to live in their own dioceses and preach, instead of collecting income from far away. Each diocese was to have a seminary, a school where future priests would be trained before they were sent to a parish. And after the council came a catechism and a single form of the Mass for much of the Latin church, which people still call the Tridentine Mass, from Trent. Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Trent is what renewal looks like when a large, old institution tries it on itself: slowly, with arguments, interrupted, and then carried out into the parishes by priests who had been trained first.

Here's the practice: one thing Trent did well. Settle, and breathe. Take one of its quieter changes: bishops were told to live among the people they served, instead of drawing an income from far away. Bring to mind one thing you look after from a distance. A friendship kept up only by text. A group you belong to on paper. A place or a person you're meant to care for. What would it mean to show up there in person this week? Choose one small step. If you pray, you can ask for help to take it. If you don't, just hold the step in mind and let it settle. The bell holds the time.

Counter-Reformation. The name later given to the Catholic answer to the Reformation, centered on the Council of Trent, which both restated Catholic teaching and reformed the church's own life. Some call it the Catholic Reformation.
Your line: reform from within. Today, instead of walking away from one thing that's broken, fix one small part of it from the inside. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Catholics receive the Council of Trent's decrees as the teaching of an ecumenical council; seminaries for training priests, which the council called for, remain the usual path to the Catholic priesthood, and the Tridentine Mass is still celebrated in some places.

original.note: Latin: the Council of Trent, from Tridentum, the city's Latin name. Tridentine comes from it.
